title: How do you dynamically route requests to different backends at runtime in Spring Cloud Gateway (`RouteLocator`)?
shortTitle: Dynamically routing requests to different backends at runtime in Spring Cloud Gateway

s1_definition.profdef: In Spring Cloud Gateway, routes are defined by a `RouteLocator`, which produces a set of routes where each route has a predicate that decides when it applies, a URI that names the backend, and optional filters. Static routes live in configuration, but dynamic routing means the route table can change at runtime without redeploying the gateway. You achieve this by supplying a programmatic `RouteLocator`, by backing routes with a `RouteDefinitionRepository` so they can be added, changed, or removed through an API or a datastore, and by refreshing the route cache with a `RefreshRoutesEvent`. This lets you shift traffic, add new backends, or reroute around failures live.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the gateway as the information desk at National Bank of India that tells each visitor which counter to go to. A static route is a printed sign on the wall; to change it you must take down the old sign and hang a new one, which means closing the desk. Dynamic routing is instead a digital board that the manager can update instantly from his office. When the loans team moves to a new counter, or when one counter is overloaded and visitors must be split between two, the manager updates the board live and visitors are redirected immediately, without ever closing the desk.
s1_definition.oneliner: A `RouteLocator` is the gateway's route table, and backing it with a refreshable `RouteDefinitionRepository` lets you add, change, or shift routes at runtime without a redeploy.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In Spring Cloud Gateway, routes are defined by a `RouteLocator`, which produces a set of routes where each route has a predicate that decides when it applies, a URI that names the backend, and optional filters. Static routes live in configuration, but dynamic routing means the route table can change at runtime without redeploying the gateway. You achieve this by supplying a programmatic `RouteLocator`, by backing routes with a `RouteDefinitionRepository` so they can be added, changed, or removed through an API or a datastore, and by refreshing the route cache with a `RefreshRoutesEvent`. This lets you shift traffic, add new backends, or reroute around failures live.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the gateway as the information desk at National Bank of India that tells each visitor which counter to go to. A static route is a printed sign on the wall; to change it you must take down the old sign and hang a new one, which means closing the desk. Dynamic routing is instead a digital board that the manager can update instantly from his office. When the loans team moves to a new counter, or when one counter is overloaded and visitors must be split between two, the manager updates the board live and visitors are redirected immediately, without ever closing the desk.

**One line to remember:** A `RouteLocator` is the gateway's route table, and backing it with a refreshable `RouteDefinitionRepository` lets you add, change, or shift routes at runtime without a redeploy.

sections.s2_technical:
The simplest routing in Spring Cloud Gateway is static, defined in `application.yml` under `spring.cloud.gateway.routes`, where each route lists an id, a URI, predicates, and filters. This is read at startup and is perfect for stable routing. But it cannot change while the gateway runs.

For programmatic routing you define a `RouteLocator` bean using the `RouteLocatorBuilder`. For example, `builder.routes().route("account", r -> r.path("/api/v1/accounts/**").uri("lb://account-service")).build()` builds a route that forwards the accounts path to the account-service instances resolved by the load balancer. This is still fixed at startup unless you make the underlying definitions mutable.

True runtime dynamic routing comes from the `RouteDefinitionRepository` interface. Spring Cloud Gateway loads routes from every `RouteDefinitionLocator`, and `RouteDefinitionRepository` is the writable one. By implementing it, you can store route definitions in memory, in Redis, or in a database, and expose an admin API that adds or removes a `RouteDefinition` at runtime. The built-in `InMemoryRouteDefinitionRepository` already supports this and is wired to the actuator gateway endpoints, so you can POST a new route to `/actuator/gateway/routes/{id}` and it takes effect without a restart.

The missing piece is cache refresh. The gateway caches the compiled routes for speed, so after you change a definition you must publish a `RefreshRoutesEvent` to rebuild the cache. You do this by calling `publisher.publishEvent(new RefreshRoutesEvent(this))`. After the refresh, new requests are matched against the updated table.

The URI of a route decides the backend. A literal URI like `http://host:port` sends traffic to a fixed address. A `lb://service-name` URI defers to the load balancer and service discovery, so the actual instance is chosen at request time, which is itself a form of dynamic routing because instances come and go. Weighted routing lets you split traffic between two backends, for example 90 percent to the old service and 10 percent to the new one, using the weight predicate, which is the foundation of canary and blue-green deployments.

A senior nuance is where to store the dynamic routes and how to keep multiple gateway instances consistent. An in-memory repository is fine for a single instance, but with several gateway replicas you need a shared store like Redis or a database plus a mechanism to broadcast the refresh event to all replicas, often through a message bus such as Spring Cloud Bus. Another nuance is safety: because routes control where money-moving requests go, changes must be authenticated, validated, and audited, and ideally staged, so a bad route definition cannot silently send payment traffic to the wrong service.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India is migrating its Payment Service to a rewritten version. The operations team wants to move traffic gradually: start by sending everything to the old payment backend, then at runtime flip a portion of traffic to the new backend, and finally cut over fully, all without redeploying the gateway or causing downtime during salary week. This is exactly runtime dynamic routing and weighted routing.

Problem 2 — When a backend misbehaves, operations wants to instantly reroute its traffic to a healthy standby without waiting for a deploy pipeline. They need an admin action that updates the live route table and refreshes it immediately.

The connection to the fix: we will model a small routing engine like Spring Cloud Gateway's. It holds a mutable list of route definitions. An admin API can add, update, or remove a route and then refresh the compiled route table. The engine matches an incoming path to a backend, including a weighted split between two payment backends.

What the code will do. There is a `RouteDefinition` with id, path prefix, backend URI, and weight. There is a `RouteDefinitionRepository` that stores definitions and supports add and remove. There is a `DynamicRouteEngine` that compiles the definitions into a route table, matches requests, applies weighted selection, and refreshes on demand. The demo starts with all payment traffic going to the old backend, then at runtime adds a weighted route sending some traffic to the new backend, then reroutes the account service to a standby, refreshing after each change.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the plain-Java dynamic routing demo
javac DynamicRoutingDemo.java
java com.bank.gateway.demo.DynamicRoutingDemo

# Real Spring Cloud Gateway: change a route at runtime via actuator
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/actuator/gateway/routes/payment-new \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"uri":"lb://payment-service-new","predicates":[{"name":"Path","args":{"pattern":"/api/v1/payments/**"}}]}'

# Apply the change (refresh the cached route table)
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/actuator/gateway/refresh
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a series of requests to the payments path and one to the accounts path, with the route table changing between phases.

Step 1. In phase one, the repository holds one payment route pointing to the old backend. The engine refreshes, so the compiled table has that route. Each of the four payment requests matches the single payment route and goes to payment-service-old. There is only one candidate, so no weighting happens.

Step 2. In phase two, operations saves a second payment route pointing to the new backend with weight 25, and reduces the old route's weight to 75. The engine refreshes, so the compiled table now has two routes sharing the payments prefix. Each payment request now matches two candidates, so the engine does a weighted pick, sending roughly three of four requests to the old backend and one to the new. The traffic split happened live, with no redeploy.

Step 3. In phase three, operations saves the account route again but with the backend changed to the standby. The engine refreshes, and the account request now matches the updated route and goes to account-service-standby instead of the original. The reroute took effect immediately after the refresh.

Step 4. Throughout, the key moment is always the refresh. Saving a definition changes the repository, but requests keep using the old compiled table until the refresh rebuilds it. This mirrors how Spring Cloud Gateway caches routes and rebuilds them on a `RefreshRoutesEvent`.

```

2026-10-24 13:10:01 [INFO] /api/v1/payments/pay → payment-service-old
2026-10-24 13:10:01 [INFO] /api/v1/payments/pay → payment-service-old
2026-10-24 13:10:01 [INFO] === Phase 2: add weighted route, 25% payments → NEW ===
2026-10-24 13:10:01 [INFO] Routes refreshed: 3 definitions
2026-10-24 13:10:01 [INFO] /api/v1/payments/pay → payment-service-old
2026-10-24 13:10:01 [INFO] /api/v1/payments/pay → payment-service-new
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
In Spring Cloud Gateway, routing is driven by a `RouteLocator`, which produces routes, and each route has a predicate that decides when it matches, a URI that names the backend, and optional filters. Static routes in `application.yml` are fine for stable mappings, but they are fixed at startup, so for runtime changes I define routes programmatically with the `RouteLocatorBuilder` and, crucially, back them with a `RouteDefinitionRepository` so the route table can be changed while the gateway is running. The built-in in-memory repository is wired to the actuator gateway endpoints, so I can add or remove a route definition through an API and the change becomes live without a redeploy.

The one detail people forget is the refresh. The gateway caches the compiled routes for speed, so after I change a definition I have to publish a `RefreshRoutesEvent` to rebuild the cache, and only then do new requests match the updated table. In my banking work at National Bank of India, this is exactly how we migrated the Payment Service. We started with all payment traffic going to the old backend, then at runtime added a weighted route that sent twenty-five percent of payments to the rewritten backend as a canary, refreshed the routes, and watched the metrics. Because the URI can be a weighted split, this gave us a safe, gradual cutover with no downtime during salary week.

The URI itself is a form of dynamic routing too. A literal address pins traffic to one host, but an `lb://` URI defers to service discovery and the load balancer, so the actual instance is chosen per request and instances can come and go freely. We also used a runtime reroute once when an account backend misbehaved: an operator changed the route's backend to a healthy standby and refreshed, and traffic moved instantly without a deploy pipeline.

The senior nuances I always raise are consistency and safety. With several gateway replicas, an in-memory repository is not enough, so I store route definitions in a shared store like Redis or a database and broadcast the refresh to every replica using Spring Cloud Bus, so they all rebuild their tables together. And because routes decide where money-moving requests go, every route change must be authenticated, validated, and audited, ideally staged, so that a careless route definition can never silently send payment traffic to the wrong service.
